opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that a drone and a humanoid robot are fundamentally different kinds of problems, even though people often lump them together as "robotics."

When DJI matured its drones, the physics of the problem was actually quite well understood. A quadcopter is, in a sense, a relatively simple system: four motors, a rigid frame, and it operates mostly in free air. The interaction with the environment is minimal. You're controlling attitude and position, and the control theory for that had decades of foundation behind it. So the challenge became an engineering and manufacturing challenge: how do you make motors, IMUs, GPS, gimbals, and batteries extremely consistent, extremely cheap, and extremely well-integrated? That's where DJI excelled. They turned a solved-in-principle problem into a product with consumer-grade reliability.

Humanoids are different on almost every axis. First, they're contact-rich. A humanoid is constantly making and breaking contact with the ground, with objects, sometimes with people. Contact is discontinuous, it's hard to model, and small errors in friction or timing can lead to a fall. Second, the degrees of freedom are much higher. You have dozens of joints, each with actuators, reducers, and sensors, and every one of those is a potential point of failure. Reliability multiplies down: if each joint is 99.9% reliable, you still have a system that fails far more often than you'd accept from a consumer product.

Third, the hardware supply chain isn't there yet. For drones, there was a huge existing ecosystem from smartphones: cheap cameras, IMUs, batteries, chips. For humanoids, things like high-torque-density actuators, durable dexterous hands, and robust tactile sensing are still being invented or are very expensive and not standardized. You can't get to DJI-level quality without a mature supply chain and huge production volume to iterate on.

And fourth, the task definition itself is open-ended. A drone's job is basically "fly where I tell you and hold the camera steady." A humanoid is expected to walk in unstructured environments, manipulate arbitrary objects, and generalize. The software side, especially learning-based control and manipulation, is still in a research phase. Reinforcement learning and sim-to-real have made locomotion dramatically better in just the last few years, but manipulation and long-horizon tasks are not yet at a level where you could say "this works 99.99% of the time."

So I'd say humanoids today are roughly where drones were before the Phantom era, maybe even earlier. The demos are impressive, but demo reliability and product reliability are very different things. Getting there will take volume, better actuators, better data, and honestly a lot of boring engineering: thermal management, cable routing, fall protection, maintenance. That boring part is exactly what DJI was great at, and it's what the humanoid industry still has to go through.

r001.rationale: It attributes DJI’s drone reliability to engineering and manufacturing, but does not mention failures after widespread customer deployment.

r002.rationale: It says drone control theory had decades of foundation, but does not identify a several-year gap before DJI found the flying-camera use case.

r003.rationale: It compares humanoids to drones before the Phantom era, but does not place them at or before the drones’ 2009 stage.

r004.rationale: It says reaching product reliability will take “a lot of boring engineering” and gives examples such as thermal management, cable routing, fall protection, and maintenance.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that a drone and a humanoid are solving fundamentally different problems, and the gap in reliability reflects that difference more than any failure of effort.

A drone lives in a very forgiving environment. The air is basically empty. The physics are well understood, the dynamics are relatively simple, and the failure modes are few. Once DJI nailed the flight controller, the gimbal, the battery management, and the obstacle avoidance, they could ship millions of units that behaved almost identically. The product converged. You could design it, test it, and manufacture it to a spec, and the world mostly cooperated.

A humanoid has to touch the world constantly. Every step is a contact event with uncertain friction, uncertain terrain, uncertain loads. Every grasp involves objects that deform, slip, or weigh something different than expected. The robot has dozens of actuators, each with its own thermal limits and wear curves, and they all have to coordinate under real-time constraints. So the number of things that can go wrong is enormous, and the environment doesn't converge. A home, a warehouse, a factory floor are all different, and they change daily.

The second issue is that we're still at the stage where the control stack is partly learned rather than fully engineered. With drones, the behavior is deterministic enough that you can reason about safety margins. With humanoids, a lot of the capability comes from learned policies, and we don't yet have mature tools for verifying them, for understanding when they'll fail, or for guaranteeing consistency across units. That's a research problem, not just an engineering problem.

Third, there's the supply chain and manufacturing maturity. DJI benefited from a decade of iteration on components that are now commodity: brushless motors, ESCs, IMUs, cameras. Humanoid actuators, especially the high-torque-density ones with good backdrivability, are still custom, expensive, and produced in small volumes. You can't get drone-level consistency when every joint is effectively a prototype.

And finally, I'd say the industry hasn't yet done the unglamorous work. DJI's reliability didn't come from a breakthrough. It came from years of field data, failure analysis, and relentless iteration on boring details. Humanoids are only now starting to accumulate that kind of operational mileage. I expect reliability to improve rapidly once units are deployed at scale and the feedback loop closes, but we're a few years away from that, and it won't be a single company solving it. It'll be the ecosystem of components, tooling, and data maturing together.

r001.rationale: It says DJI built reliability through field data and failure analysis, but does not explain that stringent targets arose from failures after widespread customer deployment.

r002.rationale: It mentions DJI’s decade of iteration but gives no several-year gap between drone technology maturing and the flying-camera use case.

r003.rationale: It does not compare humanoid development with the stage drones had reached in 2009.

r004.rationale: It says DJI’s reliability required years of field data, failure analysis, and relentless iteration on details, and that humanoid reliability depends on components, tooling, and data maturing together.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is the complexity of the task. A drone has a relatively clear objective: stay stable in the air and follow a commanded trajectory. That’s a hard engineering problem, but the operating conditions and the definition of success are fairly well bounded.

A humanoid has to balance while making contact with a world it doesn’t fully understand. If it picks up a cup, the cup might be slippery, heavier than expected, or in a slightly different position. And you need perception, planning, control, and hardware to work together. A small error in one can become a failure of the whole system.

There’s also a maturity gap. Reliability comes from repeated testing, manufacturing consistency, and learning from failures in actual use. Humanoids need much more of that cycle. A successful demonstration shows that something is possible. Doing it thousands of times without intervention is a very different milestone.

So I’d start with a narrow, useful task in a controlled environment, make that dependable, and then expand. You don’t get general-purpose reliability just by building a general-purpose body.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliability and testing generally, but does not say DJI’s targets arose from failures after widespread customer deployment.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a several-year gap between drone technology maturing and DJI finding a flying-camera use case.

r003.rationale: It does not compare humanoids’ development stage with where drones were in 2009.

r004.rationale: It recommends starting with narrow tasks and building dependability, but does not argue that commercial companies must painstakingly work through product details to achieve stable, mass-produced humanoids.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is the complexity of the problem. A drone moves through the air, and although flight looks difficult, you can stabilize it with a relatively small number of actuators and a very fast control loop. DJI made that whole system—the hardware, the software, the manufacturing—work together reliably.

A humanoid has many more joints, and it’s constantly making and breaking contact with the world. Every step involves balance, friction, and impact. Then you ask it to pick something up, and now it has to deal with objects whose weight, shape, and stiffness it may not know. A small error can propagate through the whole body.

The other piece is that reliability comes from repetition. You need a clearly defined task, lots of real-world use, and a feedback loop that turns failures into engineering improvements. Humanoids are still figuring out which tasks they should do first. To reach that DJI standard, I think we need to narrow the scope, make a useful task work consistently, and build from there.

r001.rationale: It says DJI made the drone system reliable, but does not attribute stringent reliability targets to failures after widespread customer deployment.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss when drone technology matured or when DJI found a flying-camera commercial use case.

r003.rationale: It compares humanoid and drone complexity but does not place humanoids at or before drones’ 2009 developmental stage.

r004.rationale: It recommends narrowing humanoid tasks and improving through feedback, but does not argue that commercial companies must painstakingly work through product details to achieve stable, mass-produced robots.
